cards.title: Prioritize a shortlist of business-driving keywords instead of ranking for everything
cards.summary: Start SEO planning by naming the handful of keywords that actually represent buyers, then accept you can't and shouldn't own the whole keyword universe.
cards.use_when: Keyword roadmap planning for an online store — deciding which product, category and service terms deserve page builds this quarter.
steps: Accept three realistic constraints before spending: ultra-competitive head terms dominated by enterprise brands for years are usually not worth the resources for small and mid-sized stores; holding position #1 is an ongoing cost (refresh, links) once won; and ranking for every relevant keyword is unnecessary. The presenter frames prioritization, not execution, as the hardest part of SEO.

List your business-driving keywords in tiers: (1) brand name, (2) explicit names of the products or services you sell or terms describing them, (3) for local businesses, geo-modified service terms. The source's examples: a DTC eyewear brand targets 'buy glasses online', 'affordable prescription glasses', 'home try-on glasses'; a B2B SaaS targets 'electronic signature software' and 'X alternatives'; a Houston plumber targets 'plumber near me', 'Houston plumber', 'drain cleaning Houston'.
Translate this to your catalog: pick the category and product terms that match how your buyers describe what you sell, plus competitor-alternative terms if shoppers compare you.
Deprioritize vanity and off-topic informational terms whose traffic will not reach a money page.
Revisit the list when you add product lines — every new revenue-driving page needs its own cluster (see the topical cluster card).
caveats: The tiering (brand first, product/service names second) is the source's heuristic for typical businesses, not a calculated rule.
The presenter states getting a ranking is 'half the battle'; maintaining it requires continuing work, and results are never guaranteed.

cards.title: Run the SERP intent check before writing any page
cards.summary: Google your target keyword first and let the format of the top results tell you what page type Google assumes the searcher wants.
cards.use_when: Before building or rewriting a PDP, category page, homepage or landing page for a target keyword.
steps: Google the target keyword in an incognito window and study the organic results page, not just the ads. Modern SERPs mix sponsored posts, Reddit threads, listicles, homepages, YouTube videos, AI overviews and People Also Ask accordions.

Identify Google's 'assumed search intent' — what Google believes searchers want — by the dominant format: if the top results are homepages, target the keyword on your homepage; if they are listicles, build a listicle; if how-to searches show videos, make a video.

Note mixed-intent queries, where the SERP offers several formats at once because Google itself is unsure. Example from the source: 'electronic signature software' surfaces a Reddit discussion first, then a listicle, then vendor homepages.

For mixed intent, choose between the source's two approaches: (a) adopt the majority view — if five or more results are homepages, target your homepage; (b) strategically pick the format you can realistically rank with given your domain's current authority, even if it differs from the majority.
Then match the page format to what you found, while differentiating the substance (opinions, first-hand data, original visuals) rather than copying the leaders.
Re-check the SERP periodically; formats shift and your format decision should follow.
caveats: The 'five or more results' majority test is the source's practical heuristic, not a documented ranking factor.
Search results vary by day, location and personalization; the presenter notes the SERP can differ 'depending on how Google is feeling that day'.

cards.title: Use the roundup post backdoor when you can't outrank enterprise homepages
cards.summary: Publish an objective 'best of' comparison that includes competitors so a lower-authority store can rank for a competitive commercial keyword.
cards.use_when: Merchandising or content decision when a high-value category keyword is owned by big-brand homepages and your domain lacks their authority.
steps: Confirm the problem with a SERP intent check: if major brands rank their homepages for your target term, a head-on homepage fight is likely not winnable for a smaller site.
Publish a roundup/comparison piece that reviews options including your own product and your competitors, framed as giving readers free, objective value so they can decide.

Demonstrate real methodology so the roundup is credible: a consistent review structure per entry (the source's example uses a 'best for' badge, description, screenshot, pros, cons, ideal use case), original screenshots of each option, and a stated testing claim.
Give it skimmable structure — a table of contents and a TL;DR section — because commercial-intent readers compare quickly.
Internally link from the roundup to your relevant PDP or category page so the comparison traffic can convert.
Plan to keep it updated; stale comparisons lose trust and rankings.
caveats: The source's example (GetAccept ranking a roundup over larger competitors DocuSign and PandaDoc) is a single case study, not a guaranteed outcome.
Including competitors is a real trade-off: you send some readers to rivals, so your entry must compete on genuine merits and your differentiators must be clear.
The presenter's own framing is that competitive head terms are often not worth the resources for smaller businesses — this tactic is the alternative, not a promise of #1.

cards.title: Match the SERP's format, then differentiate on substance not word count
cards.summary: Build each money page in the format Google already rewards for that keyword, and compete by covering the topic more completely instead of writing longer.
cards.use_when: Building or rewriting a PDP, category page or landing page after the SERP intent check.
steps: Copy the winning format, not the winning content: identify whether the top results are product pages, category pages, long-form posts, listicles or videos, and make your page that format. The source explicitly includes video when how-to SERPs show videos.

Ignore word count as a target — the presenter states Google does not reward a particular length. Replace 'how long should this be?' with 'what does someone searching this need to know, and have I covered it completely?'
Study competitor outlines to ensure you cover the topic at least as thoroughly, and mine the SERP's People Also Ask / questions data to answer every question in the content.

After drafting in your own words, review for semantic coverage — the entities and subtopics the top pages treat — because this supports both traditional search and AI answer surfaces. (The source uses Surfer's content editor workflow for outlines, questions and entity checks; verify current features if you use the tool.)
Differentiate on substance you can add that competitors can't: original photography, real screenshots, tested specifics, opinions and data.
Keep the page's commercial job clear — the format may be informational, but the page should still route buyers toward the product or category it supports.
caveats: The source is a Surfer-sponsored video; tool-specific workflow steps describe one interface and may change.
Quality coverage does not guarantee rankings — the presenter stresses that a great page alone is not enough for newer or low-authority sites.

cards.title: Prove first-hand experience on money pages and supporting content
cards.summary: Google's E-E-A-T evaluation rewards visible evidence that you actually used or did the thing, with Experience weighted heavily per the source.
cards.use_when: Auditing or upgrading product pages, buying guides and comparison content so they look earned rather than assembled.
steps: Add the concrete experience signals the source lists: original photos, actual screenshots (e.g., dashboards, editors, signature flows for software), step-by-step documentation from doing the thing, case studies with specific numbers, and personal anecdotes about what worked and what didn't.

Show methodology and consistency — the cited roundup structures every review the same way (badge, description, screenshot, pros, cons, ideal use case), which signals the same evaluation framework was applied to each item.
Add accountability markers: a real author byline with a photo, publish date and last-updated date. The source describes these as small details that attach a name to the claims.
Make it skimmable with a table of contents and a TL;DR for commercial comparison content.

If you lack the experience yourself, get it: use the product, or interview someone who has — the presenter suggests this could even be a reviewer found in product reviews, so you don't need to be the expert personally.
Apply the same standard to your product pages: real photos, real usage scenarios, real specs rather than generic copy.
caveats: The claim that the extra 'E' (Experience) is now the most heavily weighted factor is attributed to 'reputable SEO sources' in the video, not to published Google documentation — treat it as the presenter's reporting.
The presenter's framing of E-E-A-T is 'how Google claims to evaluate content'; it is a guideline concept, not a measurable score.

cards.title: Build topical authority clusters around each money page
cards.summary: Rank a competitive page by surrounding it with a complete ecosystem of related content on the topic, rather than publishing one isolated page.
cards.use_when: Planning the content roadmap that supports a key category page, product page or service page.
steps: Pick the money page (a category, product or service page) as the center of the cluster and define the overarching topic it belongs to.

Map every angle a buyer or learner could search around that topic. The source's hydroponics example: best systems for vegetables, for outdoor growing, for apartments, for limited space, and on a budget — the goal is coverage from every conceivable angle.

Compare two hypothetical sites: identical page quality, but one has a single page published two weeks ago and the other has the full ecosystem plus backlinks from relevant sites. The presenter's argument is that Google would clearly favor the ecosystem site.

Use a tool that maps your existing coverage against the topic to find gaps — the source describes plugging your domain into Surfer's sites dashboard with Google Search Console to see where you stand (verify current interface).
Publish in priority order of the gaps, and plan the work realistically: the presenter says one full cluster plus links can take several months of full-time work, with results possibly months later.
Interlink every supporting piece to the money page and to its siblings (see the link authority transfer card).
caveats: The comparison is a thought experiment, not data — it illustrates the mechanism of topical authority, not a measured ranking effect.
Timelines ('several months of work', 'another few months' for results) are the presenter's estimates, and he assumes product-market fit and a technically sound site are already in place.
Do not over-invest in a money page if the keyword was deprioritized by the realistic assessment above.

cards.title: Earn backlinks on educational posts, then pass the authority to money pages with internal links
cards.summary: Top-of-funnel guides are easier to link to than sales pages; transfer that link equity to product and category pages through contextual internal links.
cards.use_when: Link building and internal linking plan for an ecommerce catalog, when deciding which URLs to pitch for links.
steps: Build topical authority content first, before outreach — the presenter states he will 'die on this hill' and considers this order more important than link hunting.

Pitch the easier sell: not 'link to my sales page because I want money', but something like 'you link to a six-year-old page on nutrient solutions; I just published a new post where I tested a bunch of them'. The source argues a fresh, genuinely helpful guide makes the pitch almost impossible to refuse.
Get the backlink to the supporting blog post, not the money page.

Then internally link that post to the relevant money page with contextual anchor text. When every supporting page does this, the accumulated backlink authority flows to the money page and lifts its standing in search results.
Repeat the whole cycle for each revenue-driving page — the source describes this as a rising tide across the site.
Prefer natural links earned because content is genuinely good; the presenter names this his preference, while acknowledging that most people push back on that answer.
caveats: Backlinking is described as a large topic deserving its own series; this card covers only the funnel-transfer logic, not outreach tactics.
The mechanism for how internal links pass authority is stated as SEO practice by the presenter, not measured here.
Effort is substantial — the source estimates months of work per cluster before rankings may move, with no guarantee.

input.text:
15-SEO / search engine optimization Goes here. A realistic SEO roadmap focusing on prioritizing money pages, matching search intent, building E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness) through first-hand experience, and creating topical authority clusters that utilize internal linking to pass backlink power. Not here. • Paid ad campaign strategies or Meta Ads tracking -> 06-MEA • Setting up backend payment gateways or Shopify configurations -> 05-SET

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a structured, three-step approach to SEO (identifying keywords/intent, building E-E-A-T compliant pages, and powering them up via topical clusters and internal links) that debunks "guaranteed ranking" myths. modules: [SEO] topics: [search intent, E-E-A-T, topical authority, internal linking, keyword targeting, backlinking] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. keyword targeting / selecting core business-driving keywords (brand name, explicit product names, specific services) instead of trying to rank for everything; search intent / analyzing the SERP (Search Engine Results Page) to understand Google's "assumed search intent," identifying mixed intent queries (e.g., homepages vs. listicles vs. Reddit discussions), and adapting formatting (e.g., using a roundup post backdoor when out-branded by enterprise competitors); E-E-A-T / optimizing content to demonstrate Experience (original photos, screenshots, case studies, personal anecdotes) and Accountability (author bylines, publish dates), moving beyond simple word counts to comprehensive factual coverage; topical authority / building an ecosystem of related, interconnected content pieces around a central topic (rather than relying on a single isolated post) to signal expertise to search engines; internal linking / using supporting blog posts to earn natural backlinks (e.g., informative guides) and then passing that link authority (link juice) directly to the bottom-funnel money pages (e.g., product/sales pages) via contextual internal links.

Look for.

The SERP Intent Check: Googling a target keyword before writing to see what format Google ranks (e.g., if the top 5 results are homepages, target your homepage; if the top results are listicles, build a listicle).

The Roundup Post Backdoor: The strategy of creating an objective "best of" listicle that features competitors alongside your own product, used to rank for highly competitive software/product keywords when your domain lacks the authority to rank its homepage.

The E-E-A-T "Experience" Mandate: Proving first-hand experience by utilizing original photography, actual screenshots of software dashboards, and author bylines, specifically avoiding generic AI-spun fluff.

The Link Authority Transfer: The specific tactic of earning backlinks to top-of-funnel educational blog posts (which are easier to get links for than sales pages), and then internally linking those posts to the bottom-funnel money pages to transfer the SEO power.

Skip. Promotional pitches for the Surfer software tool and generic disclaimers about not guaranteeing #1 rankings.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard SEO execution and strategy). Volume. ~350 words.

In this video, we're going to give you a step-by-step road map to ranking number one in Google in 2026. Starting with the first lesson. Don't ever trust anyone who tells you they can guarantee ranking number one in Google. Sorry to disappoint, but that's just way beyond our control as marketers. But before you click off, I've done SEO for over a decade and I've helped brands get to the number one position with a repeatable, proven process. And what you can do is create as many winning conditions as possible on your website to give you the highest possible chance of ranking highly in Google. That's a way less sexy but more accurate way to say it. My name is Matt and I run a consultancy called Kenyon Digital where I help businesses get more traffic, leads, and sales from organic search and AI visibility. I've partnered with Surfer once again to give my three-step process for higher rankings in this video. So before we get into the nitty-gritty, we have to take realistic stock of what we're after. I'm going to give you three reality checks here. First, if you're looking to rank number one for ultra competitive terms, terms that have been dominated by enterprise level businesses for years or decades, that's probably not a feasible task. These businesses have spent years building their authority and spent millions of dollars on their content. I mean, it's not impossible, but it's probably not worth the resources, especially for smaller to medium-siz businesses. Secondly, you have to understand that it's one thing to rank number one, and it's another thing to stay number one. Once you crack that top spot for a particular keyword, especially a competitive one, you've got a target on your back, and all your competitors will be trying to outdo you in content quality and build more links than you. So, just know that getting the ranking is half the battle. Keeping it is an ongoing effort that requires regular content refreshing, authority building, and more. And thirdly, you don't need to rank number one for every keyword relevant to your business. In fact, doing so may be a waste of your resources. For any given business, there are likely thousands of potential keywords across their service offerings and content. And expecting or trying to rank all of them number one is just not realistic, nor is it necessary to have a very successful organic search presence. One of the hardest things about SEO is not really the execution. It's actually the prioritization. And that's something I hope to help you with in this video. Okay. So, our minds are calibrated. Our expectations are set. Let's get ranking. Now, I know many of you watching this already have a website, likely with some ranking keywords. Whether they're ranking high or low is a different story, but I just want you to forget about all that for a second and start with a clean slate. Ask yourself, what are the businessd driving keywords that in a perfect world my prospects would type into Google and then find me? This is going to be different for different types of businesses, but the first is almost always going to be your brand name. The next most important are likely going to be explicit names of products or services you sell or keywords describing those things. WBY Parker, a direct to consumer eyewear brand, targets keywords like buy glasses online, affordable prescription glasses, home tryon glasses. Docuign, a B2B SAS company, will target keywords like electronic signature software, signed documents online, or docuine alternatives. And yes, you want to rank for that, too. And for NYX Plumbing, a local business in Houston, Texas, target keywords might include things like plumber near me, Houston plumber, or names of specific services like drain cleaning Houston, water heater repair Houston, or sewer line repair Houston. Once you've identified your core keywords, Google each of them and really study the results page. The first thing you'll notice, if you haven't noticed already, is that in 2026, the search engine results pages, or SERs for short, look very different than they did even just a few short years ago. For example, when I Google electronic signature software, I see a series of sponsored posts, a Reddit discussion as the top organic result, a listical of the best electronic signature software platforms, and some homepages of popular software companies like DocYsine. Depending on how Google is feeling that day, you may also see YouTube video results, AI overviews, or accordion style people also ask questions. So, yeah, we've come a long way from 10 blue links. It's easy to get overwhelmed here, but our main goal is to figure out one thing. What is the search intent behind this keyword? Or put another way, what do you think people are trying to find when they search this? And perhaps more importantly, what does Google think people are trying to find when they search this? I call that last one Google's assumed search intent. And it's very important that your content meets that search intent as closely as possible. Now, I'm actually glad I use this particular query, electronic signature software, as an example because it has mixed intent. Ooh, meaning there are multiple possible intents that people can have when searching this. How do we know this? We just look at the SER. Someone searching for this term might want to eavesdrop on some Reddit discussions about the best software for e signatures. Or they might want to read a roundup post comparing a list of the best platforms. Or maybe they just want to be taken straight to a vendor's homepage. Google, despite its sophistication, doesn't quite know. So what does it do? It gives the user an all you can click buffet of options and lets them decide. But this poses a problem because I just said the most important thing is matching your page's content to the keyword search intent. So, how do you do that when the search intent is mixed?
